items.stem: In a directed response, what does the examiner mainly reward?
options: Personal opinions unrelated to the source
Writing that suits the new form, audience and purpose while using the source material
Analysis of the source’s language
Copying as much of the source as possible
items.answer: Writing that suits the new form, audience and purpose while using the source material
items.markingKey: Directed response tests the transformation of source material for a new task.

items.stem: A student is transforming Text B, an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’ into a short assembly speech written for secondary-school students. Explain two changes they will need to make to form and register.
items.answer: Form: adopt direct address and inclusive pronouns for a listening audience and spoken signposting such as ‘first’ and ‘finally’. Register: move from the source’s formal, assured and persuasive register to a direct, spoken and rousing register suited to secondary-school students.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: a relevant change of form (direct address and inclusive pronouns for a listening audience); a relevant change of register or tenor; explanation linked to the new audience (secondary-school students).

items.stem: A student is transforming Text A, an extract from a travel memoir about trekking to a mountain monastery into an email written for a close friend who lives abroad. Explain two changes they will need to make to form and register.
items.answer: Form: adopt a friendly greeting and sign-off and informal, colloquial lexis. Register: move from the source’s literary, reflective and personal register to a friendly and informal register suited to a close friend who lives abroad.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: a relevant change of form (a friendly greeting and sign-off); a relevant change of register or tenor; explanation linked to the new audience (a close friend who lives abroad).

items.stem: Read Text B, a page from a trekking company’s website. ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise] MONASTERY TRAIL – 5 DAYS | Moderate | From $640. Walk in the footsteps of pilgrims on one of the region’s most spectacular routes. ✔ Expert local guides ✔ Comfortable teahouse lodges ✔ All meals included. Day 3 is our favourite: you’ll climb above the clouds and watch eagles soar beneath your feet. “The best week of my life!” – Ana, Brazil [BOOK NOW button]’ Write the opening (about 40 words) of a magazine article written for teenage readers, based on this text. Then explain one choice you made to suit the new form.
items.answer: An opening that uses a catchy headline and standfirst and adapts a point from the source such as ‘the trek lasts five days’, in a register suited to teenage readers; explanation of one choice.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: opening clearly in the new form (a catchy headline and standfirst); register suited to the new audience; content adapted (not lifted) from the source; accurate, controlled expression; a valid explanation of one choice.

items.stem: Read Text A, a news article from a national newspaper. ‘Reservoirs at Record Low as Heatwave Grips Capital. Water levels in the capital’s three main reservoirs have fallen to 31 per cent of capacity, the lowest figure since records began in 1978, officials confirmed yesterday. From Monday, the use of hosepipes and sprinklers will be banned, and car washes must recycle at least half of the water they use. “We are not yet in a crisis,” said Dr Leila Haddad, director of the regional water authority, “but every household can make a difference.” Forecasters expect temperatures to remain above 38°C for at least another week. Critics argue that the authority has failed to repair leaking pipes, which lose an estimated fifth of all treated water.’ Write the opening (about 50 words) of a short assembly speech written for secondary-school students, based on this text. Then explain one choice you made to suit the new form.
items.answer: An opening that uses direct address and inclusive pronouns for a listening audience and adapts a point from the source such as ‘reservoirs are at 31% of capacity’, in a register suited to secondary-school students; explanation of one choice.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: opening clearly in the new form (direct address and inclusive pronouns for a listening audience); register suited to the new audience; content adapted (not lifted) from the source; accurate, controlled expression; a valid explanation of one choice.

items.stem: Read Text A, an extract from a travel memoir about trekking to a mountain monastery. ‘By the third day my legs had stopped complaining and simply given up. The path zigzagged above the cloud line, and every time I thought I had reached the top, another ridge rose ahead of me like a cruel joke. Our guide, Pema, walked as if the mountain were flat, humming to himself and pausing only to point out a vulture circling below us. Below us. I remember that more than anything: looking down at a bird in flight. When the monastery finally appeared, its prayer flags snapping in the wind, I did not feel triumph. I felt very small, and strangely grateful.’ Write the opening (about 60 words) of a script for a 60-second radio advertisement written for local radio listeners, based on this text. Then explain one choice you made to suit the new form.
items.answer: An opening that uses sound effects and voice directions and adapts a point from the source such as ‘by day three the narrator was exhausted’, in a register suited to local radio listeners; explanation of one choice.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: opening clearly in the new form (sound effects and voice directions); register suited to the new audience; content adapted (not lifted) from the source; accurate, controlled expression; a valid explanation of one choice.

items.stem: Read Text A, an information leaflet from a city transport department, ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely’. ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely. E-scooters are now available to hire across the city centre. To keep yourself and others safe: • You must be 18 or over and hold a driving licence. • Ride on roads and cycle lanes only – never on pavements. • Wear a helmet. It could save your life. • Only one rider per scooter. Fines of up to $300 may be issued to riders who break these rules. For more information, visit our website or scan the QR code below.’ You are a student who rides an e-scooter. Using material from the text, write a script for a 60-second radio advertisement written for local radio listeners (120–150 words). Base your answer closely on the text, adapting its content for your new audience and purpose.
items.answer: Indicative content: Form: sound effects and voice directions; repetition of the key message and contact details; short, punchy spoken sentences. Content selected from the source: e-scooters can be hired across the city centre; riders must be 18 or over with a driving licence; scooters must be ridden on roads and cycle lanes, not pavements; helmets should be worn; only one rider is allowed per scooter. Voice: convincingly that of a student who rides an e-scooter. Register shifted from the source’s formal, clear and instructional register to suit local radio listeners.

items.stem: What is ‘lifting’ in a directed response?
options: Removing irrelevant content
Copying phrases or sentences directly from the source without adapting them
Lifting the tone of a text
Using a quotation in an analysis
items.answer: Copying phrases or sentences directly from the source without adapting them
items.markingKey: Lifting shows little transformation and is not rewarded.

items.stem: A student writing a letter to a local newspaper written for the newspaper’s readers, based on Text A, an information leaflet from a city transport department, ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely’, copies ‘You must be 18 or over’ word for word. items.answer: It is lifting: the phrase belongs to the source’s form (information leaflet) and formal, clear and instructional register; it should be rephrased in the voice and register of a letter to a local newspaper written for the newspaper’s readers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies lifting/lack of transformation; explains the mismatch of form or register; a valid adapted version or method.

items.stem: Read Text A, a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme. ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners – thank you for coming out on such a wet evening. Look up when you leave tonight. Every flat roof you see is a field waiting to be planted. Last summer, the pilot garden on the bus depot grew four hundred kilos of vegetables, cooled the building below by three degrees and gave thirty families somewhere to meet. Imagine that on every block. Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to. So I am asking you tonight: lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness, and together we will turn this grey city green.’ Select two points from this text that would be most useful for an information leaflet written for members of the public. Then explain how you would adapt one of them.
items.answer: The pilot garden on the bus depot grew 400 kg of vegetables; It cooled the building below by three degrees. Adaptation: rephrase in a register suited to the new audience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: The pilot garden on the bus depot grew 400 kg of vegetables; It cooled the building below by three degrees; It gave thirty families a place to meet; Every flat roof is potential growing space; Some people object to the cost; Volunteers are needed, including at weekends; a valid explanation of adapting one point.

items.stem: Read Text B, a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’. ‘Nobody warns you about kilometre 30. The crowds have thinned, the energy gels taste like warm glue and your brain starts negotiating: just walk for a bit, nobody will know. I knew. At kilometre 31 a woman in a pink tutu overtook me, and something in me snapped – not my hamstring, thankfully, just my pride. I finished in 4 hours 12, which won’t trouble the record books, but I raised enough for half a ventilator. Next year, the whole thing. Tutu optional.’ Select three points from this text that would be most useful for a short assembly speech written for secondary-school students. Then explain how you would adapt one of them.
items.answer: Kilometre 30 is the hardest point; Crowds thin and energy gels taste bad; The writer was tempted to walk. Adaptation: rephrase in a register suited to the new audience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: Kilometre 30 is the hardest point; Crowds thin and energy gels taste bad; The writer was tempted to walk; A woman in a tutu overtook him and spurred him on; He finished in 4 hours 12 minutes; He raised enough for half a ventilator; He plans to run again next year; a valid explanation of adapting one point.

items.stem: Read Text B, a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’. ‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat. Twelve months later I have calloused hands, a slightly ridiculous number of chilli plants and – who knew? – actual friends. It isn’t all sunshine. The lift to the depot roof breaks constantly, the water tank leaked twice in August, and our tomatoes were demolished by pigeons. But on Saturday mornings, with the traffic grinding below and Mrs Okafor handing round her ginger tea, it feels like the only quiet place in the city. If you’re on the fence, come up and see. Bring gloves.’ In no more than 40 words, and using your own words as far as possible, summarise the main points of this text for a reader who has not seen it.
items.answer: The writer joined mainly to get out of the flat. After a year the writer has made real friends. The lift to the roof often breaks. The water tank leaked twice. Pigeons destroyed the tomatoes. Saturday mornings on the roof are peaceful. Readers are invited to visit.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: The writer joined mainly to get out of the flat; After a year the writer has made real friends; The lift to the roof often breaks; The water tank leaked twice; Pigeons destroyed the tomatoes; Saturday mornings on the roof are peaceful; Readers are invited to visit. Deduct for lifting long phrases or for exceeding the word limit significantly.

items.stem: Read Text B, an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’. ‘The evidence is now difficult to ignore. In schools that have removed smartphones from the school day, teachers report calmer corridors, fewer incidents of online bullying and, in several studies, modest gains in test scores. Of course, a ban is not a cure-all; determined pupils will always find a way, and parents understandably want to be able to reach their children. But these are problems of management, not of principle. Children deserve a few hours each day in which their attention belongs to them rather than to an algorithm. Schools should pocket the phones – and keep them pocketed.’ A student is selecting content from this text for a directed response. Which of these points is accurate?
options: The editorial calls these practical problems, not reasons against a ban
Studies show test scores doubled
The editorial opposes a ban
Bullying increased after phones were removed
items.answer: The editorial calls these practical problems, not reasons against a ban
items.markingKey: The editorial calls these practical problems, not reasons against a ban is stated in the text; the other options misrepresent it.
